title: Describe It Better
objectives: I can use enormous and tiny to tell exactly how big or small something is.
I can use narrow and curved to describe a shape.
I can use smooth and shiny to describe how something feels and looks.
I can choose a better word than big, small, or nice.
rationale: Each word in this unit replaces a vague word children already use: big, small, thin, bent, nice. That gives them a reason to choose the exact word. Size words come first (enormous, tiny, narrow), then shape (curved), then surface (smooth, shiny), so children describe from the whole thing to the details. The unit revisits describe, foggy, and chilly, because describing the weather and describing objects use the same careful word choice.

words.def: Not wide; small from side to side.
words.ex: The path through the woods was narrow.
words.ex2: A narrow bridge crossed the stream.
words.nonExample: A wide road is not narrow.

words.def: Bent like part of a circle, not straight.

words.ex2: A curved slide wound around the playground.

apps.writing: Use curved to describe a bent shape.

misuse.why: A curved line bends. A line that is straight from end to end does not bend.

words.def: Flat and even with no bumps.
words.ex: The smooth stone felt cool in my hand.
words.ex2: The lake was smooth, with no waves at all.
words.nonExample: A rough rock is not smooth.

apps.academic: Feel the smooth side and the rough side.
apps.writing: Use smooth to tell how a surface feels.

cloze2.s: The skater glided across the ___ ice.

misuse.s: The smooth sandpaper scratched my fingers because it was so rough.
misuse.why: Smooth means flat with no bumps. Sandpaper that scratches is rough.

words.def: Bright because light bounces off it.
words.ex: The shiny coin sparkled in the sun.
words.ex2: Mom polished the pan until it was shiny.
words.nonExample: A dusty old rock is not shiny.

morph.note: The e is dropped: shine + y becomes shiny.

apps.academic: Metal can look shiny when light hits it.
apps.writing: Use shiny to show what sparkles.

cloze.s: The new car was so ___ that I could see my face in it.

cloze2.s: She polished the old coin until it was clean and ___.

misuse.s: The shiny mud looked dull and dusty.
misuse.why: Shiny means bright when light bounces off. Dull, dusty mud is not shiny.

passage.title: A Walk by the Pond
paras: Lila and her dad walk down a narrow path by the pond. They see an enormous tree with curved branches. A tiny green bug sits on a smooth leaf. Then a shiny fish jumps out of the water. Lila wants to describe it all in her journal.

qs.q: Where do Lila and her dad walk?
choices: Down a narrow path by the pond
qs.why: The first sentence says they walk down a narrow path by the pond.

qs.q: What is on the smooth leaf?
qs.why: A tiny green bug sits on a smooth leaf.

qs.q: What does the word shiny tell us about the fish?
choices: It is bright when light hits it.
qs.why: Shiny means bright because light bounces off, so the fish looks bright.

teacher.overview: Children learn six exact describing words for size, shape, and surface, then use them in place of big, small, thin, and nice. The unit revisits describe, foggy, and chilly.

notes.va.enormous.adj: Put enormous on a size line past big. Use a picture of an elephant next to a mouse. Children often use huge for everything; enormous is one more word they can pick.
notes.va.tiny.adj: Tiny is smaller than small. Show a magnifying glass on a seed or an ant. Link to enormous as an opposite pair.
notes.va.narrow.adj: Use two strips of tape on the floor, one wide and one narrow. Ask which one a bike could ride on. Narrow is not the same as short.
notes.va.curved.adj: Trace curved lines in the air with arms. Link to curve and to the -ed ending: shaped like a curve. Sort objects into curved and straight.
notes.va.smooth.adj: Pass around a smooth stone and a rough one. Children should say smooth after touching, not just looking. Smooth is a feel, not a color.
notes.va.shiny.adj: Shine a flashlight on foil and on paper. Shiny is about light bouncing off. Link to the shine part of the word and to the -y ending.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'I want to describe this rock. I could say it is big, but enormous is a better word because it is taller than me. The little stone next to it is tiny. The path between them is narrow. The rock feels smooth, and when the sun hits it, it is shiny.'
discuss: What is something curved that you can see in this room?
Why is enormous a better word than big sometimes?
misconceptions: Enormous and tiny both mean big.
extend: Children go on a classroom hunt for smooth, shiny, and curved things and tell what they found.
Play 'Better Word': say a vague sentence and children replace the dull word with one from the unit.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit enormous and tiny the next day as an opposite pair, again at one week, and use the unit words in writing about animals or weather. They return in unit 12 when children compare and measure.

frames: A tiny ___ can fit in my ___.
wida.oral: Partner A describes an object in the room with two words from the unit. Partner B points to the object and says one more word to describe it.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (enorme, diminuto, estrecho, curvo, liso, brillante) are not reviewed by a native speaker; shiny may be better as brilloso or reluciente in some regions.
Ant for tiny and enormous is each other; the pair is size opposites, not strict dictionary antonyms.
